# Why a mixed DP contest is different

The hard part is not filling a table. It is deciding whether a state can retain
all information needed for the future while discarding everything else.

# Complete local contest set

| Problem | Title |
|---|---|
| A | Training Schedule |
| B | Two Carts |
| C | Prerequisite Tree |
| D | Circular Exhibition |
| E | One Diagonal Path |
| F | Matrix Chain |
| G | Hamiltonian Route |
| H | Sliding Jump Cost |
| I | Grouped Cargo |
| J | Minimum Starting Energy |
| K | Last Crystal Removed |
| L | Weighted Tree Guards |

Problems E, F, and G add dedicated grid, interval, and bitmask DP tasks. Treat
H through L are a harder second pass over one-dimensional, knapsack, grid,
interval, and tree DP. Derive each state from its contract before consulting
the editorial.

# Harder second pass

The added exercises are designed around five questions that do not arise as
strongly in A--G:

| Problem | Additional question |
|---|---|
| H. Sliding Jump Cost | Can the repeated transition aggregate be maintained incrementally? |
| I. Grouped Cargo | Which layer must remain unchanged to prevent taking two choices from one group? |
| J. Minimum Starting Energy | Is the useful state easier to define backward from the destination? |
| K. Last Crystal Removed | Does choosing the final action make the interval boundary stable? |
| L. Weighted Tree Guards | What information must a child communicate about dependence on its parent? |

For H, first write the direct `O(nk)` recurrence. Optimization should preserve
that recurrence, not replace its meaning. For I, distinguish an item layer from
a group layer. For J, notice that maximum energy upon arrival is not sufficient
to describe how much energy a suffix will require. For K, attempting to choose
the first removal makes the new neighbors depend on decisions outside each
subproblem; reverse the viewpoint. For L, a Boolean “guard or no guard” state
cannot distinguish a protected vertex from one still waiting for its parent.

# State diagnosis, not an answer key

For each local task, answer these questions before writing `dp`:

```text
What decision is made next?
Which facts about the past can affect later decisions?
What does one state mean in a complete sentence?
What is the base case, and why is it true?
Which earlier states can transition into this state?
```

Do not choose a state because it resembles a familiar template. A good state
has a precise meaning and no irrelevant history. The local editorial gives the
specific states and transitions after you have tried to derive them.

# Validate a recurrence

For every transition, prove two directions: every legal construction reaches a
state through one listed transition, and every listed transition produces a
legal construction. Then decide the iteration order from dependencies: a state
must be finalized before later states read it.

Use a tiny brute-force oracle for small inputs. Compare its answer to the DP
while changing one feature at a time: an empty choice, a maximum budget, an
infeasible prerequisite, or equal values. A mismatch usually exposes a state
definition error rather than a syntax error.

# Complexity discipline

Multiply the number of states by transitions examined per state. If one state
dimension follows a large numeric bound, ask whether the bound is genuinely
small enough. If the input is a tree or graph, include the total work across
all edges and merges; a locally plausible transition may still be quadratic.

# Implementation habits

Initialize unreachable states explicitly and keep the meaning of the sentinel
consistent. Use a wide type for scores and sums. With in-place updates, write
down whether reading a value updated in this iteration would illegally reuse
the current item or decision.

# Exercises

Attempt A through G from first principles, then H through L as the harder
reinforcement set. For each, submit a one-sentence state definition, a base
case, one transition, and the derived complexity before opening the editorial.
